01.title: Vilhena, RO, Brazil
01.hook: Is Vilhena's dry season losing critical rainfall?
01.headline: Dry-season rainfall (Apr–Sep) in Vilhena dropped by 234.5 mm since 1981 (-53.3 mm/decade).
01.context: Gateway to the Western Amazon and hub of Rondônia's grain production. Sustained dry-season precipitation loss intensifies soil water deficit during second-crop (safrinha) development and raises fire risk across the Cerrado–Amazon transition (UN SDGs 6, 13 & 15; complementary to MapBiomas land-cover series).

02.title: Ariquemes, RO, Brazil
02.hook: Are tropical nights in Rondônia getting persistently hotter?
02.headline: Annual minimum night-time temperatures in Ariquemes rose +1.82 °C since 1981 (+0.41 °C/decade).
02.context: Warmer tropical nights reduce nocturnal physiological recovery for rural workers and livestock while increasing thermal stress on perennial Amazonian crops such as robusto coffee and cocoa.

03.title: Corumbá (Pantanal), MS, Brazil
03.region: Upper Paraguay Basin · World's Largest Tropical Wetland
03.hook: Is the Pantanal biome losing root-zone soil moisture?
03.headline: Annual root-zone soil wetness in Corumbá fell -5.60 percentage points since 1981 (-1.27 pts/decade).
03.context: Multi-decade root-zone drying across the Pantanal floodplains lowers water tables, amplifies extreme wildfire seasons, and threatens biodiversity and river navigation across central South America (UN SDGs 6 & 15).

04.title: Svalbard, Arctic
04.hook: How fast is polar amplification warming the High Arctic?
04.headline: Annual mean air temperature in Svalbard surged +3.50 °C since 1981 (+0.79 °C/decade).
04.context: Global reference benchmark illustrating polar amplification: the High Arctic is warming roughly three to four times faster than the global average, driving sea-ice retreat and permafrost thaw (UN SDG 13).

methods.title: Scientific Methodology & Limitations
methods.subtitle: How GeoTrend processes NASA POWER / MERRA-2 records and evaluates statistical significance.
methods.teaser: Every result here comes from the same NASA data and the same two statistical tests, explained in full on the

nasaData.title: 01. Data Source — NASA POWER & MERRA-2
nasaData.body: All series are retrieved from the NASA Prediction Of Worldwide Energy Resources (POWER) Agroclimatology Archive (`temporal/monthly/point`), derived from NASA GMAO MERRA-2 reanalysis and satellite observations spanning 1981–2025.

aggregation.title: 02. Seasonal Aggregation & Quality Control
aggregation.body: Raw monthly readings equal to `-999` (missing data or ocean mask for land variables) are filtered out before aggregation. Incomplete seasonal windows are dropped so partial years never bias the end of a trend line. Temperatures (`T2M`, `T2M_MIN`) use seasonal means in °C; precipitation (`PRECTOTCORR`) sums monthly `mm/day × days in month` into total seasonal millimeters; root-zone soil moisture (`GWETROOT`) scales dimensionless wetness `[0–1]` to `0–100%`.

mannKendall.title: 03. Non-Parametric Mann-Kendall Trend Test
mannKendall.body: Climate series frequently contain skewed distributions and extreme outliers (such as El Niño / La Niña years). The Mann-Kendall test evaluates every pairwise comparison `sign(x_j - x_i)` for `j > i`, applies tie-group variance correction, and computes a two-sided `Z` statistic and `p`-value (`p < 0.01` = Strong Evidence; `p < 0.05` = Evidence Confirmed; `p ≥ 0.05` = Insufficient Evidence).

sensSlope.title: 04. Theil-Sen Median Slope & 95% Confidence Interval
sensSlope.body: While Mann-Kendall determines whether a trend is statistically significant, Sen's Slope estimates how fast the variable is changing by taking the median of all pairwise slopes `(x_j - x_i) / (t_j - t_i)`, accompanied by a 95% Gilbert / Hollander-Wolfe rank confidence interval and Ordinary Least Squares R².

formulas.title: 05. Mathematical Provenance & Benjamini-Hochberg FDR
formulas.body: All statistical tests run deterministically in TypeScript without external black-box dependencies. When scanning all 4 NASA POWER variables simultaneously at a single location, raw p-values are adjusted using the Benjamini-Hochberg (1995) step-up False Discovery Rate (FDR, α = 0.05) procedure to prevent multiple-testing false positives.

limitations.title: 07. Scientific Limitations & Interpretation Guardrails
limitations.gridItem: MERRA-2 Spatial Grid (~50 km): Values represent a ~0.5° × 0.625° regional grid cell, not an isolated farm rain gauge or urban microclimate station.
limitations.causationItem: Correlation vs. Causation: A statistically significant Mann-Kendall p-value proves that a directional shift occurred in the observed series above random noise; it does not isolate whether the driver is global greenhouse forcing, regional deforestation, or decadal ocean oscillations.
limitations.regionalItem: Regional Contrast & Amazon Context: Global climate change does not act uniformly — different regions and seasons can warm or dry at distinct rates. In Rondônia and the Pantanal, pairing NASA POWER climate trends with land-use series (such as MapBiomas) supports environmental education and territorial planning aligned with UN SDGs 6 (Clean Water), 13 (Climate Action), and 15 (Life on Land).
limitations.autocorrelationItem: Serial Autocorrelation & Minimum Record Length: Positive lag-1 autocorrelation (`r1`) can inflate Z-scores in short records. GeoTrend enforces a strict 15-year minimum (`n ≥ 15`) and flags records shorter than 30 years or with high lag-1 autocorrelation.
